The reviewer describes the genie game feature: a wheel spins, stops on a high prize, and then the genie moves the wheel so the outcome becomes a spin tag with a much lower prize. This is a claim that the game overrides or manipulates the displayed outcome of the wheel, concealing how results are actually determined — the wheel's stop is not what it appears. The wheel itself is also a chance-based reward delivery system with variable outcomes. No real-money stake is mentioned, so Gambling does not apply.

labels.label: P_IllusionOfControl
labels.span: whe the wheel spin after stopping on a great price the genie move the wheel to a spin tag, and then the prices after the spin are way lower than the original price, from 100 million with 5x multiplier to a 48 million
labels.rule_applied: definition / vs Alleged rigging boundary rule
labels.rationale: The span asserts the game manipulates the wheel's outcome after it stops, downgrading the displayed prize — the game conceals how outcomes are determined, deceiving the player about the result.

labels.label: P_RewardMania
labels.span: whe the wheel spin after stopping on a great price the genie move the wheel to a spin tag
labels.rationale: The spin wheel is a chance-based, unpredictable reward delivery mechanism; under the vs Alleged rigging rule, the rigging claim does not nullify Reward Mania, so both apply under R9.

parsed.analysis: The review reports three technical malfunctions introduced by an update: crashes when opening gifts or trading, lag preventing pokeball throws, and lag/freezing in PvP and rocket battles where the opponent keeps attacking while the reviewer's game is frozen. Everything described is attributed to bugs and performance faults. Gift-opening and trading are mentioned only as features that crash, with no description of any obligation, donation, or reward mechanic behind them. The PvP freeze describes a malfunction causing losses, not a game rule penalising exit or absence, so R11 applies. No dark pattern mechanic is described.

The reviewer complains about three things. First, a 30-second wait to connect to a match: this is matchmaking/queue time arising from the operation of the service, not an in-game timer gating play, so it does not meet Wait to Play. Second, rewards that look generous but are 'just for show': no mechanism of delivery is described, so this is an evaluation of reward value, not Reward Mania. Third, weapon upgrades and perks are difficult to get and the player is 'stick battling to win': the reviewer describes having to keep battling repeatedly as the route to progress, which names the repeated activity (battling) tied to advancement, satisfying Grinding. 'Rob you of your time' is a general evaluation and codes nothing on its own.

labels.label: T_Grinding
labels.span: Its difficult to get weapon upgrades or any percs others you stick battling to win
labels.rule_applied: definition; boundary rule vs Slow Progress
labels.rationale: The span names the repeated activity (battling to win) as what the player must keep doing to obtain upgrades, i.e., repetitive play as the means of progress.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes Clash Royale's trophy ladder: after 8k trophies they repeatedly face the same powerful cards (mega knight, pekka, golem), which is play against other players, so Competition applies. They also state the game is 'pay to win' and that skill alone won't move you higher, which is the Pay to Win low-level pattern under Pay to Progress. The complaints about cards needing rebuffing and being spammed are balance grievances; nothing says a purchased item lost value after acquisition, so Power Creep does not lift. 'You have to go out of your way to be annoying to actually win' describes player conduct, not a game incentive rewarding dishonest or harmful play, so Encourages Anti-Social Behavior does not apply.

labels.label: S_Competition
labels.span: all you play against after 8k trophies is mega knight,pekka, and golem
labels.rationale: The reviewer describes facing other players' decks on a trophy ladder, i.e., the game pits players against each other.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: its also pay to win and usually doesn't let you get higher from just using skill
labels.rationale: States directly that spending grants advantage and that advancement is not achievable through skill alone.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes several mechanics. First, 'diamonds' are named as a premium-style in-game currency, but the span concerns customer service failing to compensate diamonds lost to a game element not appearing — a bug complaint, and no real-money conversion is described, so Intermediate Currency does not apply. Second, 'you don't have to pay to win' explicitly invokes pay-to-win: the reviewer frames paying as the route to winning while noting it is not mandatory, which establishes a paid advantage contrast. Third, 'don't buy from this game beyond the pass' names a purchasable pass, which under R5 is a battle pass / recurring fee instance. Fourth, 'Get friends and a team and trade lives' describes an existing resource-exchange mechanism between players already in the game, which is Reciprocity (not Forced Fellowship, since no recruitment of new players is described). The customer service complaint about the missing game element is attributed to a malfunction and codes nothing under R11.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: It is a fun game, you don't have to pay to win.
labels.rule_applied: Pay to Win [low-level]; Free alternative boundary rule
labels.rationale: The phrase 'pay to win' explicitly describes spending money as a route to winning; the free/paid contrast establishes the paid advantage exists even though the reviewer says it is optional.

labels.label: M_RecurringFee
labels.span: I suggest after this cust. svc experience that you don't buy from this game beyond the pass.
labels.rationale: The game contains a purchasable pass, which is an explicit instance of a recurring fee under R5.

labels.label: S_Reciprocity
labels.span: Get friends and a team and trade lives.
labels.rule_applied: definition; vs Reciprocity boundary under Forced Fellowship
labels.rationale: Players already in the game exchange lives with teammates, a resource-transfer favour mechanism between existing players.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer enjoys the game and lists suggestions, but two suggestions describe existing mechanics. 'only 5-10 minutes for a new life' implies lives currently regenerate on a slower timer, an imposed wait to play. 'just because you miss a day doesnt mean that you need to start over on your daily prizes' describes a daily login reward streak that resets if a day is missed — an active daily reward mechanism with a penalty for missing, per the boundary rule that design penalties apply even when the reviewer frames them as complaints. 'small and unnecessary tasks like celebrating' is a quality gripe with no mechanic coded.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment
labels.span: maybe only 5-10 minutes for a new life
labels.rationale: Implies lives currently regenerate on an in-game timer slower than the reviewer would like — an imposed wait before playing again.

labels.label: T_DailyRewards
labels.span: just because you miss a day doesnt mean that you need to start over on your daily prizes
labels.rule_applied: definition / boundary rule vs Playing by Appointment
labels.rationale: Describes a daily login reward streak with an active consequence for missing a day: the prize progress resets to the start.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes ads shown inside the game (rewarded or interstitial video ads in Township) that cannot be dismissed: there is no close button, tapping anywhere redirects to the store, and returning to the game leaves the ad screen stuck, forcing the player to kill the app. Two mechanics are present. First, the player is compelled to sit through advertisements with no way to exit, which is forced ad viewing. Second, the interface obstructs the opt-out: the close control is absent and any tap acts as a store redirect, meaning the dismissal control is effectively removed and interaction is routed toward a purchase surface. The 'stuck' phrasing could suggest a glitch, but the design described (no close mark, tap-to-store) is presented as how the ads behave, and the underlying behaviour is a forced, undismissable ad with a misdirecting tap target rather than a technical fault.

labels.label: T_Advertisement
labels.span: recently after seeing the ads, there is no way to close it. No cross mark on the screen , if you try to click anywhere on the screen it takes you to store.
labels.rationale: The player is compelled to view in-game advertisements with no means of dismissal, satisfying 'forced to watch ads'.

labels.label: M_UIMisdirection
labels.span: there is no way to close it. No cross mark on the screen , if you try to click anywhere on the screen it takes you to store.
labels.rule_applied: vs Attention-directing without an opt-out (second arm)
labels.rationale: The close control is absent and any tap routes to the store instead of dismissing, obstructing the opt-out and redirecting interaction toward a purchase surface.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer's main point is a feature request: they want the game to save progress and purchases so nothing is lost on deletion. Under R12, a suggested feature does not itself trigger any label. However, alongside the suggestion the reviewer describes an existing mechanic: their accumulated in-game purchases and hard work would be forfeited if they deleted the game, and that prospect is what keeps them attached ('I really don't want that to happen'). This is accumulated investment raising the cost of leaving, i.e., Invested/Endowed Value. Unlike the counterexample where the player had already lost the account and was disengaging, here the investment is actively operating on the reviewer's choice to stay. Nothing else in the review describes a mechanic: no timers, no ads, no payment gate described as currently functioning.

labels.label: P_EasyToGetHardToLose
labels.span: I know if I deleted the game I would lose everything my in-game purchases and my hard work I really don't want that to happen
labels.rationale: The reviewer's accumulated purchases and progress make exit costly; the fear of forfeiting that investment is what keeps them from deleting the game, which is invested value operating on the decision to leave.

parsed.analysis: The review is a glowing overview of Lords Mobile. Most of it is praise for graphics, storyline, and strategy depth, which are quality evaluations with no mechanic described. The one concrete mechanic named is real-time combat against other players: 'the thrill of battling other players in real-time combat,' which describes the game pitting players against each other. That matches Competition's definition directly. No monetary, temporal, or other psychological mechanic is described: nothing about purchases, timers, daily rewards, ads, or collection systems appears in the text.

labels.label: S_Competition
labels.span: the thrill of battling other players in real-time combat
labels.rule_applied: definition / Alt. def.: 'The game makes you compete against other players.'
labels.rationale: The game places players in direct real-time combat against one another, which is competition by definition; assigned irrespective of the reviewer's positive framing (R7).

labels.span: to have any change at progressing you need to purchase

parsed.analysis: The reviewer praises the tactical design but describes one concrete mechanic: the game runs on an energy system, and once energy runs out progression stops until a fairly long real-time recovery timer refills it. parsed.analysis: The reviewer reports that troop requesting from their clan stopped working after an update and asks for a fix. While troop requesting would normally describe a Reciprocity mechanic (donating/requesting resources among players), the reviewer attributes the behaviour to a malfunction caused by an update: 'It needs to be fixed.' Under R11, behaviour attributed to a bug or technical fault is not coded, since dark patterns are deliberate design choices. No other mechanic is described.

The review contains two distinct strands. First, the reviewer describes buying poke balls with real money and then observing that captures fail more often, forcing them to burn through balls faster and repurchase: an allegation that the game tunes outcomes to drive purchases, i.e., concealed manipulation of results. The payment also directly buys the means of continued play, and the paid purchases name an in-game item bought with real money, though no currency conversion is described, so no Intermediate Currency. Second, the edit reveals that the review itself was written and posted under the player's name without their knowledge: the game published content as the player. The boundary rule on Friend Spam / Impersonation explicitly covers a store review written under the player's account.

labels.label: P_IllusionOfControl
labels.span: since I started purchasing, items "poke" balls that when I tried to make a capture that they keep breaking out so I go through the balls faster so I have to purchase more
labels.rationale: The reviewer asserts the game engineers capture failures once purchases begin, i.e., outcomes manipulated on a hidden schedule to drive more purchases.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: so I go through the balls faster so I have to purchase more
labels.rationale: Continued play depends on repeatedly buying the consumable items that enable captures, which the game is alleged to deplete deliberately.

labels.label: S_FriendSpamImpersonation
labels.span: I DID NOT WRITE THIS REVIEW.....I DIDN'T TALK TO SEVERAL PLAYERS BECAUSE I DO NOT KNOW ANYONE
labels.rule_applied: Destination of the message boundary rule
labels.rationale: A review was published under the player's name without their authorship, an act performed through the player's own account identity.

The reviewer complains that levels take a week to pass and that tasks are impossible unless boosters are purchased. The first part describes slow progress, but does not name a specific repetitive activity the player must perform (farming, replaying, a task cycle), so under the Grinding vs Slow Progress boundary it does not qualify as Grinding. The second part directly states a pay wall: tasks cannot be completed without buying boosters, which is Pay to Progress — payment is presented as the required route past an obstacle. No other mechanic (timers, currencies, chance systems, social features) is described.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: way too many impossible tasks unless you buy boosters
labels.rationale: Tasks are stated to be impossible without purchasing boosters, making payment the condition for progress.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer praises the game and compares its monetization favorably to other games. The key mechanic described is spending real money ($20) on items/purchases in the game, with bingo giving 'twice the number of your purchase' — this describes real money being converted into in-game currency/credits whose exchange rate obscures the true cost, which is Intermediate Currency (Premium Currency). The mention of 'different modes and events' names events but describes no schedule, expiry, or pressure operating on the player, so no temporal or FOMO label. Payment is never tied to progression being blocked or slowed, so Pay to Progress does not apply. The comparison about getting more for your money is a value judgment on pricing, not anchoring or a purchase-friction mechanism, so no Easy to Purchase.

labels.label: M_IntermediateCurrency
labels.span: If your spend $20 on some item you get less then what your actually hoping for, but on here bingo gives you twice the number of your purchase
labels.rule_applied: Premium Currency: 'Exchange rate between real money and in-game currency disguises the real price of items.'
labels.rationale: Real money ($20) is exchanged for in-game purchase credit whose amount ('twice the number of your purchase') is expressed through the game's own conversion rather than a direct price, establishing the money-to-currency conversion.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes a limited-time event in MONOPOLY GO! They were close to completing it (3 tasks left toward a 525-dice reward), ran out of dice, and saw the event carried a '2 Days left' timer. When they logged back in after sleeping, the event had changed and their progress toward the reward was gone. Two mechanics are active: (1) a game-set clock governing when the event and its rewards are available, with rewards forfeited when the window closes — the schedule operates on the player and is tied to reward loss, which is Playing by Appointment. (2) A partially completed goal whose near-completion kept the player engaged and whose loss is the felt harm — Endowed Progress, the partially-completed-goal arm of Easy to Get, Hard to Lose. The F2P/trust comments express general dissatisfaction with monetization but describe no specific purchase mechanic, so no monetary label. Running out of dice is a resource constraint but no regeneration timer or wait is described, so no Wait to Play beyond the event clock already coded.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment
labels.span: it said 2Days left. Now just logged in after sleeping and the event is now changed.
labels.rule_applied: definition; boundary rule vs Fear of missing out (reward expires on the game's clock and the span describes the schedule and the loss)
labels.rationale: The event runs on a countdown set by the game and the reward was forfeited when the window closed, forcing play within the game's schedule or losing the reward.

labels.label: P_EasyToGetHardToLose
labels.span: The latest event I was about to get 525 dice as reward, I had 3 left to go and I ran out of dice
labels.rationale: The reviewer was three tasks from the reward and frames the near-complete progress as the wasted investment, the partially completed goal the design uses to hold engagement.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes three mechanics. First, the game rewards inviting friends and getting them to join via Facebook — recruitment of new players for in-game rewards, even though the reviewer complains the rewards stopped; the mechanic is still described as present in the game's design (R7/R8 code the mechanic, not the evaluation of its payout). Second, dice are the stake in a chance-based loop: the reviewer played max bet and got no shut downs or bank heists, describing a randomized outcome system — but no real money is mentioned, so this codes the variable reward delivery, not Gambling. Third, sticker drops are all duplicates, i.e., repeated unwanted drops from a randomised pool, which is Reward Mania delivery language; the reviewer does not describe compulsion to complete the album itself, so Complete the Collection is not assigned. The login failure is a technical fault (R11/R2) and codes nothing.

labels.label: S_ForcedFellowship
labels.span: Suddenly I get no rewards for inviting friends and getting them to join facebook
labels.rationale: The game rewards players for inviting friends to join, which instantiates the Social Pyramid Scheme indicator; the complaint is that the reward stopped, but the recruitment mechanic is described.

labels.label: P_RewardMania
labels.span: when I finally had more than 500 dices and played max bet, absolutely NO LUCK! No Shut downs and no bank heists. Stickers are duplicates all the way
labels.rationale: Unpredictable outcomes from dice betting and duplicate drops from a randomised sticker pool describe chance-based reward delivery sustaining repeated attempts; no monetary stake is described, so Gambling does not apply.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes a deliberate interface behaviour in 8 Ball Pool: on opening the game or the 1v1 section, the UI auto-scrolls to and pre-selects the highest-stakes table the player's coin balance allows. They call it a 'Dark UX' trick designed to cause accidental mis-clicks so players lose their coin balance and then have to buy more. Three mechanics follow: (1) a purchase action defaulted by the interface with accidental-spend intent, which is Easy to Purchase (Default To Purchase / Accidental Purchases); (2) the interface directing the player toward a selected option against their intent, which is UI Misdirection; (3) the implied real-money purchase of replacement coins ('forced to buy real ones'), where coins are the object bought with money, which is Intermediate Currency. The betting itself is ordinary 8 Ball Pool match wagering, not a chance-based purchase, so Gambling does not apply. The 'rigged' accusation is about the UI defaults, not about manipulated match outcomes, so Illusion of Control does not apply.

labels.label: M_EasyToPurchase
labels.span: it automatically scrolls and selects the highest possible bet table based on your coins. This is a cheap "Dark UX" trick to force accidental mis-clicks so players lose all their hard-earned coins
labels.rule_applied: Accidental Purchases; Low Barrier / Default To Purchase
labels.rationale: The game pre-selects the highest-stakes table as the default action, engineering accidental entry into a large spend with no opt-out step; the player must actively change the selection to avoid it.

labels.label: M_UIMisdirection
labels.span: the user interface is completely rigged. Every time you open the game or go to the 1v1 section, it automatically scrolls and selects the highest possible bet table
labels.rule_applied: definition: interface focuses attention on specific options against the player's intent
labels.rationale: Auto-scrolling to and highlighting the highest-bet table is the interface directing attention and selection toward the option that benefits the game at the player's expense.

labels.label: M_IntermediateCurrency
labels.span: so players lose all their hard-earned coins and are forced to buy real ones
labels.rule_applied: Purchases denominated in currency boundary rule: currency is the object acquired
labels.rationale: Coins are bought as replacements for lost ones, i.e. real money converted into the in-game currency, establishing the conversion relation.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes three mechanics. First, an assertion that the randomness is tuned against the player: 'the rng is so obviously against you' claims the game conceals or manipulates how outcomes are determined, which is Illusion of Control rather than a mere losing streak, since a rigged-RNG claim is made. Second, the free-versus-paid contrast: playing without spending actual money is 'not rewarding', meaning smooth advancement effectively requires payment, which is Pay to Progress. Third, the level economics: at around level 100 each attempt costs 2200 coins while a win barely recoups that stake. This describes the currency being spent within the game economy, but the review never shows real money being converted into coins, so Intermediate Currency's transaction-direction rule is not satisfied. The coin drain per level is part of the pay-to-progress pressure (payment becomes the route to keep playing), not a separate currency conversion, and no wait timer, reward schedule, or other pattern is described. No search is needed; the mechanics are clear from the text.

labels.label: P_IllusionOfControl
labels.span: the rng is so obviously against you it's crazy
labels.rationale: The span asserts the game manipulates the determination of outcomes via tuned RNG, which the boundary rule codes as Illusion of Control rather than a mere unlucky run.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: it's not rewarding playing the game without spending actual money.. at around level 100 it costs 2200 but if you win the level you'll barely make that back
labels.rationale: The 'without spending actual money' contrast plus per-level costs exceeding winnings establishes that the free route falls short of smooth advancement, making payment the practical path to keep progressing.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes a base-builder where events are contests between players that are effectively unwinnable without spending. Two explicit claims: 'no opportunity for a general player to win an event' and 'Zero skill pay to win', with money (30k) named as what it takes to win. This is Pay to Win (payment grants competitive advantage) over a competition structure (events pitting players against each other). The phrase 'Same old same old grinder' is a general characterisation of the game as repetitive with no specific repeated activity named and no link to a described task cycle, so under the Grinding boundary rule it codes nothing. No currency conversion, chance mechanics, or scheduling are described.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: there is absolutely no opportunity for a general player to win an event. Zero skill pay to play. Zero skill pay to win.
labels.rationale: The span states payment, not skill, determines winning, which is the Pay to Win indicator: money purchases in-game advantage.

labels.label: S_Competition
labels.span: there is absolutely no opportunity for a general player to win an event
labels.rationale: Events are contests players win against one another, so the game places players in competition.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing a sticker/card album mechanic in Dice Dreams. They were two cards short of completing an album for a grand prize, bought a paid deal that 'promised' new cards, and received duplicates instead. This carries several mechanics: the album is a collection the player is compelled to complete; completing it is tied to spending money on card deals; the deal delivers cards from a randomised pool (duplicates possible), which is a chance-based delivery with a real-money stake; and the low drop rate of needed cards is what sustains the purchase loop. The 'Free Cash' promotion is out-of-game marketing and excluded under R13. No wait timers, daily mechanics, or social mechanics are described.

labels.label: P_CompleteTheCollection
labels.span: I had two cards left which would grant me the grand prize for completing an album
labels.rationale: The player is driven to complete a full card album, with the missing pieces framed as the goal pulling them toward purchase.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: I had two cards left which would grant me the grand prize for completing an album, so i bought a deal
labels.rationale: Progress toward completing the album is pursued through a real-money purchase of a card deal.

labels.label: M_Gambling
labels.span: i bought a deal which promised i would get NEW cards, and all i got were useless duplicates
labels.rationale: Real money was spent on a card deal whose contents were chance-based, yielding duplicates rather than the needed cards.

labels.label: P_RewardMania
labels.span: all i got were useless duplicates
labels.rationale: Duplicate drops from a randomised card pool describe unpredictable reward delivery, sustaining repeated attempts at the needed cards.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes a gacha game where each patch reduces free rewards and shifts the meta so frequently that players are effectively forced to pull for new characters to deal damage. Pulls are the gacha draw mechanic, which is Reward Mania. The pull pressure is monetized: 'forcing us to pull for new characters' combined with 'the game is getting more and more pay 2 win' ties real money to chance-based character acquisition and to in-game advantage. The meta constantly shifting so older characters no longer suffice is the recency-qualifier form of Power Creep: value of already-owned characters diminishes as new ones become necessary. The complaint about a bad background picture is a quality gripe, not a mechanic. 'Less rewards per patch' describes reward value, not delivery, so it adds nothing beyond what's coded.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: basically forcing us to pull for new characters if we want to actually do damage. the game is getting more and more pay 2 win
labels.rationale: Spending (pulling) is described as granting combat advantage, and the reviewer explicitly calls it pay to win.

labels.label: M_Gambling
labels.span: basically forcing us to pull for new characters if we want to actually do damage. the game is getting more and more pay 2 win
labels.rule_applied: Loot Boxes: spending real money to play a game of chance for a reward
labels.rationale: The pull is a chance-based mechanic and the 'pay 2 win' framing supplies the monetary stake in the same span.

labels.label: M_PowerCreep
labels.span: the Meta changes more and more every single day basically forcing us to pull for new characters if we want to actually do damage
labels.rule_applied: boundary rule: recency qualifier attached to a capability requirement
labels.rationale: Constant meta shifts mean only new characters deal adequate damage, devaluing characters the player already owns, mirroring the 'new enough to deal damage' worked example.

labels.rule_applied: Gacha mechanics like pulls, rolls, banners [indicators]
labels.rationale: Pulls are named outright, which is an indicator instance of Reward Mania regardless of the stake.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer's account covers several things, some in scope and some not. 'Nothing like what's advertised' is about external store/marketplace advertising, which R13 excludes. 'Teeming with micro transaction menus' describes a high volume of purchase solicitation, but no mechanism of friction reduction, no insufficient-funds prompt, no default selection — volume of offers alone codes NONE under R2 per the Purchase solicitation boundary rule. What is concretely mechanical: after a point the game 'encourages players to attack each other', which is direct player-versus-player design, and there is 'a huge gap between p2w and f2p', meaning spenders gain advantage over non-spenders in that competition. That is Pay to Win in the competitive context. No grinding schedule, no random reward delivery, no timers or daily mechanics are described.

labels.label: S_Competition
labels.span: players are encouraged to attack each other
labels.rationale: The game design actively pits players against one another, satisfying the canonical definition of Competition.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: there's a huge gap between p2w and f2p
labels.rationale: The span explicitly describes paying players gaining an advantage over free players, which is Pay to Win.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes an update that removed 'open silver' and player-vs-player combat from Total Battle. Two mechanics are coded as currently present. First, meaningful growth requires spending: 'You have to spend to have any meaningful growth' is a direct pay-to-progress statement. Second, the update devalued what players had already bought: spending is described as made 'pointless' by the update and players 'screwed... who wasted money on this game', which is a purchased investment losing value through a game update, i.e., Power Creep. The PvP removal itself is the removal of Competition, not its presence, so Competition is not coded (R12). Easy to Get, Hard to Lose does not apply: the reviewer reports investment lost and advises others not to play; there is no reluctance to leave or investment pulling the player back (per the counterexample). No search needed.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: You have to spend to have any meaningful growth
labels.rationale: Progress in the game is stated to require spending money.

labels.label: M_PowerCreep
labels.span: You have to spend to have any meaningful growth and then they go and make it all pointless by getting rid of any player vs player
labels.rationale: Value purchased with real money was rendered pointless by an update, i.e., acquired investment devalued after purchase through a game change.
